\section*{Individual manipulation: the plurality upper scale and normalization gaps}

\subsection{Definitions and mathematical statement}
\paragraph{Shared notation.}Standard number systems are denoted by $\mathbb N,\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R,\mathbb C$; index ranges, computational models and specialized notation follow the cited problem source and the definitions below.


Neutrality means that relabeling alternatives relabels the chosen outcome in the same way. A dictatorship always follows a designated voter\textquotesingle s top choice. Distance from dictatorship is the probability of disagreement under the prescribed profile distribution; $M_i(f)$ measures profitable manipulation by voter $i$.
\paragraph{Statement recorded in the supplied source.}
Let $f$ be a neutral social choice function for $n$ voters and $m$ alternatives, and let $M_i(f)$ be voter $i$'s manipulation power. For $m=3$, if $f$ is $\varepsilon$-far from dictatorship then $\sum_iM_i(f)\geq C\varepsilon^2$. Can the current $\Omega(1/n)$ lower bound on $\max_iM_i(f)$ be improved; can neutrality be replaced by $f$ being far from having range of size at most 2; and does an analogous theorem hold for $m>3$, perhaps with a bound polynomially weaker in $m$? \href{https://doi.org/10.4171/owr/2008/01}{[S2]}
\paragraph{Scope qualification.}
The exact normalization of manipulation power and profile measure require the source. All three extension questions are retained.
\paragraph{Source status.}
The supplied catalogue labels this record open. Its source-status metadata was checked against the supplied snapshot on 2026-10-11. This import does not independently establish current open status or mathematical correctness. The catalogue literature assessment is dated 2026-08-21.

\subsection{Short English statement}
Improve individual-voter manipulation bounds, weaken neutrality, and extend the theorem beyond three alternatives.

\subsection{Sources}
\begin{itemize}
\item[S1] Ulam AI and the UnsolvedMath Contributors, UnsolvedMath: A Curated Collection of Open Mathematics Problems, record 30000894 (OWR-1782-004). Catalogue curation and metadata: CC BY 4.0. The supplied source question is retained; definitions and the English summary are editorial additions.
\url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/ulamai/UnsolvedMath}.
\item[S2] Combinatorics (2008), Oberwolfach Reports, DOI 10.4171/owr/2008/01, pp. 5--78
\url{https://doi.org/10.4171/owr/2008/01}.
\item[S3] Mossel--Racz, quantitative theorem
\url{https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.5888}.
\item[S4] three-alternative quantitative theorem
\url{https://doi.org/10.1137/090756740}.
\textit{Underlying Oberwolfach Reports material retains its source-specific licence, including CC BY-SA 4.0 where applicable; see THIRD\_PARTY\_NOTICES.md.}
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Verbatim supplied catalogue question}
Let $f$ be a neutral social choice function for $n$ voters and $m$ alternatives, and let $M_i(f)$ be voter $i$'s manipulation power. For $m=3$, if $f$ is $\varepsilon$-far from dictatorship then $\sum_iM_i(f)\geq C\varepsilon^2$. Can the current $\Omega(1/n)$ lower bound on $\max_iM_i(f)$ be improved; can neutrality be replaced by $f$ being far from having range of size at most 2; and does an analogous theorem hold for $m>3$, perhaps with a bound polynomially weaker in $m$?

\section{Primary-source normalization}
In the original report $M_i(f)$ is the probability of a profitable randomly
chosen new report, averaging over a uniform random profile and an independent
uniform complete order for voter $i$. The supplied upstream original-statement
paraphrase describes the probability that a profitable report exists. Keep
these separate: denote the latter by $E_i(f)$ and let $m!$ be the number
of possible orders. Conditioning on a profile, if there is a profitable report
there are between one and $m!$ of them. Therefore
\[
E_i(f)/m!\le M_i(f)\le E_i(f).
\]
This is an exact elementary comparison, but its loss is factorial in $m$.
It cannot by itself extend a polynomial-in-$m$ existence-probability theorem
to the report's random-misreport quantity. All three source questions remain
in scope, rather than being replaced by one of these different normalizations.

\section{Attempt at the individual-voter scale}
We rederive an upper example for three alternatives. Let $f$ choose a
plurality winner, breaking any tie according to voter 1's complete ranking.
This deterministic tie rule is neutral: relabeling carries vote counts and
the tie-breaking ranking together. It need not be anonymous.
Let $C_a$ count votes having alternative $a$ first. If every pair of counts
differs by more than two, the winner has a margin at least three and no
single changed vote can change it, since a pairwise count difference changes
by at most two. Thus, for every voter, both $M_i$ and $E_i$ are at most
\[
\Pr[\exists a\ne b:|C_a-C_b|\le2].
\]
Here is a complete $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on this probability, with deliberately
loose constants.

Fix a pair $a,b$. For each uniform independent ranking its top is $a,b$
or the third alternative with equal probability. Let $T$ be the number
of tops in $\{a,b\}$; then $\mathbb ET=2n/3$ and
$\operatorname{Var}T=2n/9$. Chebyshev's inequality, proved by
$\mathbb E(T-\mathbb ET)^2\ge u^2\Pr(|T-\mathbb ET|\ge u)$,
gives $\Pr(T<n/3)\le2/n$.
Conditionally on $T=t$, the difference $C_a-C_b$ is a sum of $t$
independent fair signs. Its largest atom is at most $\sqrt{2/(t+1)}$.
To verify this bound, put $b_j=\binom{2j}{j}/4^j$. The recursion
$b_{j+1}/b_j=(2j+1)/(2j+2)$ and
$(2j+1)^2(j+2)\le4(j+1)^3$ imply inductively
$b_j\le1/\sqrt{j+1}$. The largest even-$t$ atom is $b_{t/2}$;
for $t=2j+1$ the largest atom is $b_j(2j+1)/(2j+2)$.
Both obey the asserted bound. There are at most five integer values between
$-2$ and 2, so
\[
\Pr(|C_a-C_b|\le2)\le 2/n+5\sqrt{6/n}.
\]
A union bound over the three unordered pairs gives
\[
M_i(f)\le E_i(f)\le B_n:=6/n+15\sqrt{6/n}.
\]
Of course probabilities may also be bounded by one; the displayed estimate
is useful asymptotically.

\paragraph{The example stays far from every dictatorship.}
For a fixed voter $j$, define $g_j$ to be plurality among the other $n-1$
voters, with ties resolved using one fixed other voter's ranking. For $n\ge2$
this is independent of voter $j$'s ranking, hence
$\Pr[g_j=\text{top}_j]=1/3$. If all pairwise counts among the other voters
differ by more than two, adding voter $j$ cannot change the winner, regardless
of the two tie rules. Therefore
$\Pr[f\ne g_j]\le B_{n-1}$ and
\[
\Pr[f\ne\text{top}_j]\ge 2/3-B_{n-1}.
\]
This holds for every $j$, so these neutral rules are, for example,
$1/3$-far from every dictatorship for all sufficiently large $n$, while
every individual's power is $O(n^{-1/2})$. This rederives the upper-scale
obstruction described in the report. It neither improves the universal
$\Omega(1/n)$ lower bound nor proves that either endpoint is sharp.

\section{Attempt to weaken neutrality and extend the alternative count}
For any neutral rule on $m$ alternatives under the uniform profile measure,
the output is uniform: relabeling profiles preserves their probabilities
and permutes any specified output to any other. For a fixed two-element
set $A$, a rule with image in $A$ can agree with $f$ only where $f\in A$,
a probability $2/m$. This is achievable by following $f$ there and choosing
a fixed element of $A$ elsewhere. Thus the distance from the class of rules
with range of size at most two is exactly $1-2/m$ when $m\ge2$.
This proves a necessary quantitative consequence of neutrality, not its
converse and not a replacement for its uses in a manipulation proof.
The attempted extension by conditioning on an existing profitable report
also stops at the factorial loss $m!$ above; a polynomial dependence on
$m$ needs additional structure controlling which reports work.

\section{Adversarial audit and remaining gaps}
The audit checked the tie rule's neutrality, the fixed-voter independence
in the distance estimate, the two-unit count-change bound, and the factorial
normalization loss. No computation was needed for these proofs.
The later Mossel--Racz primary abstract states a nonneutral quantitative theorem
for profile manipulability and general numbers of alternatives. This is relevant
historical context, not a full comparison proof for all three questions and
this precise $M_i$. No assertion that all the 2008 questions remain presently
open is made. The new universal individual lower bound, its sharp order,
and a complete theorem with the requested weaker hypotheses and polynomial
alternative dependence are not established here.

The proved material is a rederivation of known or auxiliary facts rather than a substantiated new advance on the original target. The known plurality upper scale is rederived, but no improved universal individual lower bound or complete weaker-hypothesis/general-m theorem with the original random-misreport normalization is proved.
